rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch on provable trade-press rails: "How Brex built card issuing and local-currency reimbursement in 50 countries" asks for licenses, partners, FX, and a named exec before anyone opens their mouth. B is cleaner than most AI angle sets, but "A 50-country buildout tests what a $12.3B private fintech can afford" turns two supplied facts into a burn-rate story Brex did not give you evidence to sustain. That is useful as an internal danger note, not a pitchable angle unless the company is ready to hand over economics.
gaps_in_A: "The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" decorates the before-state. The update says local reimbursement, not wires, FX losses, or a month-end mess.

"Enterprise customers pushed Brex, the startup card company, to go global" overstates the identity shift. The facts say enterprise customers requested global spend management and many customers are venture-backed startups, not that Brex is still chiefly perceived as a startup card company.
The competitive angle still rests on "50 countries" before the country list, currencies, and live availability are nailed down. A reporter will test that number first.
gaps_in_B: "A 50-country buildout tests what a $12.3B private fintech can afford" is the dangerous one. It asserts an affordability/economics story from valuation and undisclosed profitability alone.
"has mostly been fought on features and pricing in the US" is not in the update. That is a fake category history unless sourced elsewhere.
"means dozens of regulatory and banking arrangements" states the plumbing answer before Brex has supplied the plumbing. Make it a proof question, not a claim.

It throws away the most founder-useful trade route with "a customer-story angle without a customer is an invitation to invent one." The correct move is to require a named finance-team customer, not refuse the buyer workflow angle outright.
